utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic. Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey. So I think we can start. Are there any preliminaries? No. This guy hasn't got any protective measures? No?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He does need a caution, though, I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Janjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal, to this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to give evidence. Our rules require that before you start your testimony, you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text of this solemn declaration, which is equivalent to an oath is being handed to you. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Janjic. Please make yourself comfortable. Have a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The procedure here is quite simple and uncomplicated. Mr. McCloskey will ask you a series of questions and then he will be followed by the various Defence teams. If we all cooperate, and that includes you by keeping your answers as concise and as to the point as possible, you have a good chance of finishing your testimony today. But before you start giving evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a matter that is of concern to you. You lived through these events, some of which are the subject matter of this indictment, and there is a possibility, however remote or unlikely it might be, that in the course of the examination-in-chief and cross-examination, questions may be put to you which, if you answer truthfully, could expose you possibly to criminal proceedings. Now, as in many, if not all, criminal jurisdictions throughout the world, we also have a provision in our rules which gives you a limited right to ask to be exempted from answering such questions if they are put to you. It's not an absolute right, in the sense that we can accede to your request and grant you an exemption, or we can simply disagree with you and order you to answer such questions. If we choose the latter, that is, if we order to you answer such questions, then you have a further right. Provided that your answers to such questions are truthful, then whatever you say in answering such questions cannot be used against you and will not be made use of in any subsequent proceedings that there could possibly be. As I said, I am alerting you to these rights that you have under the rules, not because I'm expecting such questions but because such questions could be put to you, and then you would need to know what your rights are. All right? Have I made myself clear enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Janjic. He's all yours, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and everyone, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Janjic. Can you first of all tell us your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Mile Janjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Labourer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what country do you currently live in?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I currently live in Austria, and work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you testify in the Blagojevic case in May 2004 as a --

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that as a Defence witness called by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to listen to the audio of your testimony in the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: After that date, yes, but only last Sunday, two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you also give a statement to the BiH state prosecutor on February of this year?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have a chance yesterday to see a transcript in your language of that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you listened to your testimony, did you find any areas that you wished to clarify with me, that we went over?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Besides those clarifications which I will go over, if you were asked those same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I believe they would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you testify truthfully in that prior trial?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you stand by your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. As I had mentioned to you, I'll read a summary of that testimony. Then we'll go over the clarifications. But as I -- as I'm reading the summary, if you found that I've made a mistake or there is something you want to change, feel free to interrupt me. I know we've gone over this once before, but sometimes translations change or you may have thought about something. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. In July 1995, Mr. Janjic was a member of the Bratunac Brigade military police. In the period leading up to the fall of Srebrenica, on 11 July, Mr. Janjic was on duty engaged in his normal military police tasks. On 11 July 1995, late in the afternoon, just before dark, about 10 to 15 members of his military police unit were assembled by Momir Nikolic and told to go to the Hotel Fontana. Mr. Janjic did this and met with persons identifying themselves as the personal security for General Mladic, and those people assigned his group of Bratunac MPs to provide security around the outside of the Hotel Fontana. Later that evening, after negotiations were held at the hotel, Mladic's security people assigned Mr. Janjic and other Bratunac Brigade MPs to provide security for rooms upstairs in the hotel. Mr. Janjic and other Bratunac Brigade MPs provided security all night and left in the morning of the 12th and reported back to the military police building. At the military police building on the morning of 12 July, Mr. Janjic saw Mirko Jankovic, the commander of his unit, and his deputy, Mile Petrovic. Mirko Jankovic told him that Momir Nikolic would be calling and giving him a task. Shortly thereafter, someone came into the room and stated that Momir Nikolic called and stated that the military police should go to Zuti Most. Mirko Jankovic then told the ten or 15 MPs gathered there to go to Zuti Most. Mr. Janjic went with the group of MPs, and when they arrived at Zuti Most, they met Momir Nikolic. Momir Nikolic told them to move towards Potocari, that he would catch up with them there. About ten minutes later, when the group had reached Potocari --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really doing this hesitatingly. However, we never received the summary of the statement. The 92 ter summary. I've double checked this rather than interrupt at the outset, but we haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the position with all the other Defence teams? I see everyone nodding. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was working on it up until the last minute this morning. It's just a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we move? I can understand your -- but shall we move, notwithstanding? Okay. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe there is a requirement either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's not the point, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me see where I left off. Momir Nikolic told them to move towards Potocari and that he would catch up with them. About ten minutes later, when the group had reached Potocari, Momir Nikolic met the group and told Mile Janjic specifically that his task that day would be to assist Colonel Jankovic. Mr. Janjic did not know who Colonel Jankovic was. Momir Nikolic then pointed out Colonel Jankovic standing nearby. Mr. Janjic then walked over to Colonel Jankovic and reported to him. Colonel Jankovic told him that buses and trucks would be arriving to take the Muslim civilians from Potocari to Kladanj. Colonel Jankovic said that it would be his job, meaning Colonel Jankovic's, to count the number of Muslims transported out of Potocari and that it would be Janjic's job to help him do this and that more military police would be available to assist in this process. Colonel Jankovic told this to Mr. Janjic in the morning, before any buses or trucks had arrived. Mr. Janjic and Colonel Jankovic were about 100 metres towards Bratunac from a large gathering of Muslims. Mr. Janjic carried out this task all day, the 12th of July, and all the next day, the 13th of July. On the first day, he counted 9.000 and several hundred Muslim women and children leaving Potocari. A member of the civilian police named Milisav Ilic was also involved in counting people. During these two days, Mr. Janjic did not see any Muslims assaulted or abused in any way. Mr. Janjic did see men separated from their families. The process of separating men from their families began when the first people were boarding the buses on 12 July. Officers who Janjic did not know were issuing orders to uniformed men that Janjic did not know to separate the men from their families. These uniformed men identified themselves to Janjic as being from the specials, and Janjic knew this was an abbreviation for the Special Police unit that was under the MUP. Mr. Janjic noticed that the separated men were being taken to the other side of the street. He asked one of the Special Police why this was happening, and he was told that it was on the orders of General Mladic. During the day, Mr. Janjic noticed Momir Nikolic was present in Potocari and saw him talking to members of the Special Police. Mr. Janjic also saw General Krstic and his entourage in Potocari the first day as well as General Mladic. Later in the afternoon, buses arrived and the men who had been separated were put on those buses and driven off in the direction of Bratunac. This occurred farther down from the area where the women and children were getting on the buses. Colonel Jankovic told Mr. Janjic to count these separated men as well as the women and children. Mr. Janjic stated that between 10 and 15 buses were loaded with men that day, the 12th of July. Mr. Janjic does not recall now the exact number of men that were placed on each bus on the 12th but he does remember it was over 50 persons per bus. Mr. Janjic did not give an estimate of the number of men separated on the 13th because the buses came in several rounds and he could not recall how many buses actually transported Muslim men out of Potocari that day. The transportation of people continued on the 12th until about dusk and Colonel Jankovic was present in the area the entire day. In the late afternoon, Colonel Jankovic told Mr. Janjic that the same work would continue the next day. Near the end of the work that day in Potocari, Momir Nikolic came by and ordered Janjic and others to report to the outside of the military police building in Bratunac when the job was finished. So after the evacuation ended for the day, Mr. Janjic and other Bratunac Brigade MPs went back to Bratunac and reported to the building of the military police. Mr. Janjic and the other MPs were ordered to continue evening security detail at the Hotel Fontana. Mr. Janjic and other MPs walked across town to the Hotel Fontana and began the same security job they had done the night before. The next morning, they walked back to the military police building and received the assignments from Momir Nikolic to go back to Potocari and carry on the work from the previous day. When Mr. Janjic returned to Potocari, he saw the same group of Special Police as the previous day. Shortly after he arrived in Potocari, more buses and trucks arrived and Colonel Jankovic arrived as well. And they all continued the work they had done the previous day, counting the people moving out from Potocari. Colonel Jankovic did not give him any new orders, but at one point Colonel Jankovic came over and told them to pay more attention to the counting. The work on July 13th continued as it had the previous day. Men were separated from their families and transported towards Bratunac. Bratunac MPs went with some of those buses and returned shortly after leaving. Mr. Janjic asked one of his colleagues why he had returned so quickly. His colleague told him that the Muslim men were taken to the school in Bratunac and were being guarded there. Mr. Janjic found this strange and asked a Special Police officer what was happening and Janjic was told that the task was to finish and close the Potocari check-point as soon as possible and that there were not enough vehicles to carry all the men onward but that other vehicles would come for them shortly. On the 13th, Momir Nikolic came and went as he had the day before and Colonel Jankovic stayed in Potocari the entire day. Near the end of the day, on the 13th, Colonel Jankovic ordered Janjic and others to take a vehicle in the direction of Srebrenica, and if they found any Muslims, to tell them to come to Potocari and that vehicles would come and take them to Kladanj. Colonel Jankovic told Janjic to tell the people not to panic and that everything would be all right. Mr. Janjic carried out that order near dusk that day. He came across a couple of dozen Muslims, mostly women, and told them to go to Potocari so they could be taken on to Kladanj with the others. Mr. Janjic returned from the area of Srebrenica to Potocari where he saw Momir Nikolic. Momir Nikolic told him and the other Bratunac MPs to report to the front of the military police building. Mr. Janjic and the others did so, where they again met with Momir Nikolic. Momir Nikolic told them to go into town and help secure the Muslims detained in the schools and on the vehicles near the school. Mr. Janjic and other Bratunac Brigade MPs stayed up all night in Bratunac guarding buses full of Muslim men. At one point, he heard a man shouting from the direction of the school and it sounded like he was putting up resistance. Shortly after that, he heard automatic gunfire and the shouting stopped. Mr. Janjic did not see anyone hurt or killed in Bratunac that night. During the night, between about 10.00 p.m. to midnight, Momir Nikolic came by and told them to continue working. On the morning of the 14th, soldiers arrived at this location. They were wearing black overalls and black bandanas and some of them had dogs. Some of these men got on to the buses and the buses began leaving. When all the buses left the area, Mr. Janjic went home and got some rest. While the witness was in Potocari, he saw that the Muslim civilians were given some food. The witness did not receive any food while he was in Potocari on the 12th and 13th. During the night of 13 July and the morning of 14th July, Mr. Janjic and his colleague from the MPs provided some water and bread to some of the Muslims on a bus. That's the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that correct, according to your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would have a couple of corrections. Perhaps I could have had something to just note a few things down. If I understood it correctly, I don't know if that was correctly interpreted, it said, "We left after the first evening of security." It says, "Around noon they went to the police," and then it continues, "In the morning they returned to the police."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you -- what you actually remember happening just so we understand, on that point?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In the morning, when it got light, we left in the direction of the police and everything else I stand by, but it's unclear to me what's being referred to at 12.00, if it was correctly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which morning are -- were you talking about? What day? The morning of which day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the morning of the 12th, the first time that I went to the police, the first time that all of this in Potocari was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I also have some more things, this number 9.000 something, it is said "women and children." That's what I understood. But I would like to add, women, children and men. This figure that was mentioned, 10 to 15.000 around the buses at the end of the day, buses that are going in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It is unclear to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is an error on the page 12 line 4, this is 10 to 15.000. I don't know, is it about the buses or about people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope it wasn't buses. I would imagine we are talking about people, but I don't know. I mean, I'm not the one to clarify that. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you can handle this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you talking about 10 to 15.000 people or buses?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Buses. 10, 15 buses, not thousand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right that explains it. So there were no thousands involved. All right. Thank you, Mr. Janjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janjic, I want to go over three things, clarifications, that I think we had talked about before, and the first one can be found on the transcript of the previous trial on page 9852 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey, because when Mr. Zivanovic intervened, the witness was about to answer a question that you had put, and so let's go back. The witness had just explained about these 10 to 15 buses at the end of the day, buses that were going in the direction of Bratunac. And then you asked him, "Okay. Anything else?" And then he said, "It is unclear to me" -- and that's where he was interrupted. If he could finish that sentence, that answer, yes, Mr. Janjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we got interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there something else you wanted to explain? Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The detail was unclear to me from the second day that you mentioned. This is the 13th. About the buses that we are talking about, that at one point the buses returned quickly, that they went to Bratunac, to the school, that I learned from my colleagues. I understood that the colleagues were escorting the buses to the Bratunac school and that I asked colleagues or I asked the policemen from the Special Police where they were going, to which I would say that my colleagues together with those members of the Special Police were escorting the buses to the school in Bratunac. This is all that I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say colleagues, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: When I refer to colleagues I mean members of the military police. This is how I frequently referred to them, that they were together in coordinated action, that they are being escorted by the military police and the Special Police that happened to be in in those few days at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say escorted do you mean escorted by being inside the bus or by escorting from the outside?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: This was the usual practice, not only with the men. It was the usual practice with all, including buses that took away women. On the first day and the second day, that the army always well, call them soldiers or military police or the police, the Special Police that happened to be there involved at that moment, always escorted those buses. Inside would be one or two mostly in the front, in the immediate vicinity of the driver of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Anything else from the summary that you wanted to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go over to a couple of the clarifications or changes that we had talked about prior to court. And the first is on page 9852, beginning lines 12 -- excuse me, page 9808, beginning lines 1 through 3. And that segment, you testified that Momir Nikolic had told you that on the night of the 13th, your group would work until midnight and then the work would be over. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did Momir Nikolic actually tell you that the work would be over at midnight?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you read in your statement to the state prosecutor on that same subject? And do you remember what you said to the state prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did read that. I didn't really understand him. I understood him to say that the job Momir said would be finished, he promised that the job would be finished at midnight, that the buses would come, that those men would go. I understood him to say that that would be over at midnight, but it wasn't over at midnight. It was over only on the following day in the morning. So there was a mistake there. I don't know if I didn't hear him correctly or if it wasn't translated, but in any case it was over in the morning and not at midnight. It was promised, though, that this would be finished in the course of the night, at midnight, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to another correction and it's on page 9852, beginning line 12, and at the testimony, at the Blagojevic trial, you had stated that you did not know about men at the Bratunac stadium on the 13th of July, and in your interview with the state court, you did provide information about the stadium. Can you explain that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. From what I recall of those preparations for the Blagojevic trial, Mr. Mike Karnavas asked during the proofing for me to say or speak about only what I saw, about where I was, and what I'm sure about, not to discuss things that I had heard. In the sense that all of that would be just getting away from the topic. So just to state the facts, where I was, what I saw, who I talked about. I wasn't there, though. I didn't see it. But I did hear about it, though. And I understood that I could not really say that then. I didn't have the opportunity. Just like this time some things will also be left unsaid. It will always be like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And one more clarification and on page 9814, beginning line 8, you testified that some soldiers arrived in Bratunac on the morning and that you did not know who they were. But it appears in your statement to the state prosecutor, you identified those people. Which is -- which is correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I think that both are correct, if we take the first thing, I didn't know them but I stand behind the fact that I don't know who they are. But then again there was speculation that they maybe looked like those members of the Special Police. That was how we called them, the real Special Police members. We had two names for that formation actually. Perhaps what was dropped out was that they resembled or they looked like that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned you had two names for the Special Police. Can you tell us what those names were?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At that time, in all the events, we all knew that the Special Police existed, the Special Police, and this Special Police, you know, I can give you my opinion, the opinion of many. You know, it's a quite positive opinion about their professionalism and all. There was a lot of praise for them. And we also knew about the existence of those so-called deserter formations, this is what we called them, that were joined on to the regular forces of that honourable Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then, tell us, you said you saw men being separated when the people first started getting on the bus. Who was doing the separating?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You know, there was the presence of the Special Police there. Well, let us find some way to call them the original Special Police. There were fewer, fewer of them. And also there were large groups of that what we would call the deserter detachments of the Special Police, you know, that were joined on to these other forces, the deserters if I can call them that, who were within the Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But who, if you know, was doing the separation of men from their families?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You know, this other group, those deserters from the Special Police, who were there, of course, as part of the regular Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know, but we need you to tell us who was doing the separation, just in particular, so it's clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Not to go by groups or formations, so the answer would be the Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see members of the deserter unit actually physically separating the men from their families?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know the nickname of one of the supervisors of the Special Police that was present in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew one of their commanders. I don't know what -- if it was a platoon, a company, a squad, from some earlier events in 1992. I didn't have the opportunity in my previous appearance here in the Tribunal to -- I simply didn't have the opportunity and I wasn't sure and I'm not sure now. I don't know the first name, I don't know the last name, I know the nickname. Maybe that's part of the name of the person under the name of Mane or Manic. That could be the nickname or the last name. I cannot really guarantee about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you give this information about Mane to the state prosecutor back in February?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But from what I was able to read yesterday, it's not anywhere there, but I'm sure. I don't know why it's not included. I'm sure that during the trial from June, of this year, that question was put in the hearing, it was answered. Then, in February, and also in the Tribunal, a certain photograph of that person was shown, one photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I haven't asked you about your -- you testified in a trial this year in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About these same events?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we haven't been able to show you a transcript or an audio of that trial, have we?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When -- did the state prosecutor show you a picture of a person when you told him you remembered a nickname Mane?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The nickname Mane or Manic, and I was shown a photograph by him. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you recognise the person in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I did. Also because of the fact that I know that person from way back 1992, he also, you know, came to my house a couple of times. He was the commander, at that time, too, of some so-called special unit, I don't know. It was also the Special Police, it was described as a unit during the fall of Kravica. They were sent from the Bijeljina direction to help out the Serbian people in Kravica. They spent the time there from before the new year until the very fall of Kravica, the 7th of July -- no, the 7th of January, 1993. You know, our contact was for over seven days, ten or more days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So where were you living in that period of late 1992 and 1993 when you had contact with this person you recognised?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You know, before 1992, then the whole of 1992, until Christmas, the 7th of January until the entry of those bloodthirsty Muslim groups into Kravica, the burning of my village. That is when I go to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did I show you a -- the same picture you'd been shown by the state prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, you've said you have -- you had more photographs but you showed me just one, but it just happened by chance that it was the same one. Although you didn't talk about the same person. You said, "Out of a number of photographs, I'm going to show you one."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a look at that photograph, and see what you think. It's 65 ter number 1936, and it will be in Sanction just so we don't have any of the information on the other exhibit. It's at page 60 in e-court. Has that picture come up on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recognise -- do you recognise the person depicted in that picture?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You know, that is the person that we were talking about a bit earlier with the nickname, or the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you see him on -- or excuse me, when did you first see him?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Out of those two dates, I cannot really guarantee which one it was or if I saw him on both those dates. I saw him on several occasions and always at the same place, mostly at the exit in front of that group of Muslims at the very ramp. I am just using that vocabulary, it's not literally a ramp. It's just like a police tape in red and white. It's like an imagined ramp where the Muslims were going down in groups, going to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I think that he was helping for everything, to flow smoothly, according to my aspect, to prevent a stampede from happening, it was a large group of people, it was impossible to load them all into vehicles. Well, that was my conclusion. I didn't have any personal contact with him other than just a brief greeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see Momir Nikolic talking to him ever?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. Momir -- I didn't see any of the officers issuing any orders to him or anything. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me try to clarify some of the numbers, and I know this can be difficult but let's talk about the first day, and I'm just talking about the men, the number of buses you saw separated men get on. Today, can you give us your best estimate of the number of buses you saw men, separated men, get on on that first day, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: What I remember is what I've said, the number, I really couldn't change that now. It's difficult to make an estimate. This is a group of 10, 15, 11, 9, scores of buses, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified last time, as we know from the summary, that it was over 50 men on each bus. Can you give us any better estimate than that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, we could calculate that on our own. If it's ten buses, then times 50, or over 50 people, probably 70 most likely, because I remember that from the samples taken earlier on the 12th in the morning, in a period of one and a half hours or two hours of counting, in the buses, where the samples were taken, there were no men, I think there were just women, and if by the volume of the body we take that and each one of them had some kind of luggage, and then I could really estimate that you would have the same number of men as -- as the number of women seated, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly what you just started to say, that you were taking in the morning, you were sampling by counting each person on the bus. Can you explain how you did that and how it changed?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The first order, that first contact with Colonel Jankovic was to count persons being loaded into the vehicles, I'm talking of buses, trucks and the rest, into the vehicles. And he said that that assignment needed several people, that he was going to ask Nikolic to include more police officers, colleagues, for that assignment. We were literally going into the buses, in the majority of the cases, I'm thinking of the colleagues, they would be standing at the front and the back door; they were counting, adding up the numbers, given to me, and I was the one who was recording them. I myself was also going inside, when I didn't manage to count because it was getting more and more crowded, I would even enter the bus and try to count in order to have an as precise figure as possible because I understood that or I took that assignment very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So counting those individuals, did that change later, where you didn't count individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That changed when the numbers of buses increased, there was a terrible crowd there and it became particularly complicated and compounded by the separation of men from women, was there an ever increasing crowd because there was an increasing number of the police present, they came in ever-greater numbers. As a result of that, I suggested to Colonel Jankovic, because I concluded based on my previous experience that the numbers were more or less the same, that we apply the method of sampling. So we would actually count on the basis of the number of vehicles not of individuals, and later on, in due time, we would arrive at the number of individuals through the number of vehicles recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned the term or the word -- the number 70. How did you reach that number in response to my question about men?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: This is not a precise number. I'm not sure. But when I have in mind those large trucks, the numbers were 170, but it was mostly women and children who were boarded on to such large trucks. But I stand by the numbers concerning the buses. It was 70 and not 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know how many men or how many passengers those buses were designed for, to actually sit in?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: These were classical buses with some 52 to 54 seats. These were not double deckers, but the regular ones, numbering 52 to 54 seats. Therefore, you had the seats and you had the aisles, and of course, it's from 15 to 20 persons who could fit there, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you saw the buses filled with only men, were there people standing in the aisles?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had to see that because I was counting buses one by one, but I was quite close to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many of the buses, roughly, had men actually standing in the aisles?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question in how many -- how many of the buses, I would say all of the buses, if that was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Thank you. Okay. Now, let's go to the 13th. Can you give us a -- you weren't -- at your trial testimony, according to the summary, you had a difficulty giving an estimate. Let me ask you this question: Based on what you saw on the 13th, well, were men separated on the 13th as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us in your view was it more men or less men that were separate -- than the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: If I had the time, I would substantiate it with facts because we have the description where the men were on the first day. There was the white house on the right-hand side, a yard full of people and in addition to that, these 10 to 15 buses were fully boarded. That's what was recorded. For the second day, I don't know if there is the record of that. I described the white house, the yard, and the section of the road toward Bratunac. So looking at the right road side of the road to Bratunac and then also the meadow across from there. So by far more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on the 13th, it was by far more than on the 12th, separated men?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you get -- can you tell us any closer, how much more? Was it twice as much, three times as much, four times as much? Any -- what would be your best estimate, if you can estimate? I don't want to you speculate.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is speculation now, but in my estimate, as an eyewitness, certainly two or three times more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. At the time of this, did you know a Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you know him? What was his full name, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I lived in Bratunac. One could say that I lived in the immediate vicinity of the Bratunac SUP. I know about Ljubisa Borovcanin, as the commander of our SUP. I don't want to go into that structure of commanders, chiefs, and the top leadership of the SUP, but I know that in Bratunac, he was deemed an honourable man, an uncorrupted police officer, and I'm speaking about the period preceding all these events. I also know that in a period of time, he was away from Bratunac. The story around the town was that somebody had sold him that deserter detachment, that somebody had given him this thankless task of commanding this unit. Therefore I knew that he was at the top of the special units of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see him around Bratunac or Potocari on those days from the 11th through the 14th or 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I already said that. I really don't recall seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And another thing I want to clarify from -- well, from your testimony. You mentioned the name of a civilian police officer that was also assigned to count. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: A civilian policeman by the name of Milisav Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you see who gave him the job to count?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see him report to anybody or speak to anybody about counting or the job he was doing that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It all boiled down to this brief remark by Colonel Jankovic which I didn't see, but I presumed that they had some sort of contact, some sort of comparing of the figures. They explained what he said and...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us some more detail about that? Because you said you didn't -- you didn't see it. How did you know that, first of all, the civilian police officer -- actually I should use his name, Milisav Ilic, how did you know he was counting like you were?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I knew that from a previous event. That's to say, in the morning, when I was taking a sample, when I'm -- or when we are counting literally person by person, we were counting person by person, I noticed the presence of Milisav Ilic, I noticed that he was making notes. I don't know whether we came to that idea at the same time, but he also came down to that figure of -- the number of individuals that could be -- that could fit into a bus, and I was under the impression that he never counted the individuals, that from the start he was counting buses. Maybe he had his own average that he used, but he was interested in knowing the sum that I arrived at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where does the Colonel Jankovic come into this?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In that -- that particular dialogue took place much later, perhaps on the following day, when he was telling us, "You should take more care counting because there are some discrepancies." And on the basis of that, I presumed that he may have had a look at his figures, that's what I concluded, and if he said what he said, I believe that to be correct, true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to have to put some names on to the "he"s and the "him"s and the "us"s here, so it's very clear for the record. Okay? When Jankovic made this comment to you, who else did he make it to?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Milisav Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so is that the person you're referring to when you say, "He," "His" numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what unit was Milisav Ilic part of?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Even before the war, he was a member of the MUP of the police. At that point, he worked in the public security station in Bratunac as a policeman. Before the war, he worked in Srebrenica. I suppose that the Srebrenica and Bratunac MUP were merged then, and I know that after the war, he resumed the police duties in Srebrenica. Now I believe he's retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember what he was wearing, what Ilic was wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The blue camouflage police, the way they had. Perhaps I could have a look at the photographs, and then I recall their uniforms during the war, the blue police camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, I want to skip ahead to the point that where we ended in the summary that finally on the morning of the 14th, the buses leave Bratunac and I believe you finally get a chance to get some rest. At some point after that, did you go to Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Following the night on the 13th, on a given date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you remember about that? When, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I have never been sure of the date, whether it was the afternoon of the 14th. I know that it was in the late afternoon hours. And it was either the 14th or the 15th. I can't be sure. But in the late afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what happened in the late afternoon hours?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I happened to be in front of the police building. I don't know whether somebody informed me of the details. I cannot tell you anything. I happened to be there. A vehicle was already ready there, a Pinzgauer, and the task was that we should board the vehicle. I heard that from a colleague of mine, Slobodan Mijatovic, one of the lower-ranking or the lowest-ranking commanding officers of the police. We were told that we had a mission to accomplish and that we should set off, and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we just need to clarify, do you mean he was as a colleague was a military police from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the lowest-ranking commanding officers of the military police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall receiving orders from anyone besides him, to do this?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't think there was anybody else there at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who else do you remember going with you in this truck that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was a group of six, seven individuals. Four persons excluding myself is -- I really can identify. As for the others, I don't remember them. Let's take the driver, Milovan Mitrovic first. He was the head of the party. Then Slobodan Mijatovic. Then in the back seat behind me, there was Mladen Blagojevic. I know about that. And there were a couple, few colleagues, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know where you were going when you got in this truck?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We set off in the direction of Kravica-Konjevic Polje-Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then where?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Without any stops, without any task that was apparent to me or anything by which I could conclude what the purpose of our trip was, we arrived in Zvornik and later on in -- we passed Zvornik, and then later on in a smaller place, and I read the sign post Rocevic or Rocevici, I'm not sure, I know where the place is, we pulled over to the left road side, when facing Zvornik, and switched the engine off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, was there a bridge near this place?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I know from personal knowledge, which has nothing to do with these events, I know that several minutes drive beyond there is the Sepak bridge, which is the bridge where the -- bordering with the Republic of Serbia, across the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this road you're on above Zvornik, how would you describe that road? Was it a main road, was it an off -- an off road?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You mean the road that we were driving along or the road where we pulled over?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The road you were driving along, right before you turned over.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That was the main Zvornik-Bijeljina road. We stopped ahead of the bridge. I knew that the bridge was there, but of course we weren't able to see it where we stopped because from that place called Rocevici or Roncevici [phoen], it would take several more minutes driving to reach the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, which way did you turn off the main road driving north? Left or right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I said that we turned left, from the Zvornik-Bijeljina road. We crossed -- we turned left off that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how far did you travel until you stopped after your left turn?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: A dozen, couple of dozen metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you stop?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We stopped on the road side next to a building I presume to be a school. Actually I'm sure that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you see at that school?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything at that school. I saw in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. What did you see in front of the school?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I saw a group of people. I saw a UN APC, a personnel carrier. And that group of people. That was all. Of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What colour was the UN APC?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: White.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you recognise anybody in that area personally?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Of the persons who were there, if that's what you're asking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did you personally recognise that was there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I personally recognised the police commander, Mirko Jankovic. I recognised a colleague, a military policeman, by the name of Zoran Zivanovic. Those are the persons I could identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to recognise any of the soldiers from any particular unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As for that other group of 10 to 15 soldiers of the Serbian army that I saw outside the building, let's say in the yard, in a meadow, close to that building, as I was performing these police duties, I could recognise them as members of the Bratunac Brigade. And I state this for a fact, that I could know, judging by the faces of the persons, that they were members of the Zenica company, which was part of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that group of men from Zenica part of a particular battalion of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. There are some of them in the 1st Battalion and in the 2nd Battalion too. I believe that there is a company in each of the battalions, but I cannot state with any certainty where. I know that there are some of them in both battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is it about them being from Zenica that -- can you explain that, how men from Zenica are there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: These were members of the Bratunac Brigade. But we referred to them as Zenicani, the Zenica people, that's because they came from Zenica in 1992 with their families as refugees from that area. There they joined the Serbian army and became part of that establishment, although setting up their own units, platoons, companies, et cetera. And this was the situation throughout the war. They had their own companies and platoons that were then part of battalions, brigades, and the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm almost finished but it's break time and hopefully within five or ten minutes I'll finish up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We're still at -- we just got to the Rocevic school. Is there anybody else or any other persons that you saw there that you could help us recognise, either their identity or their unit, besides what you've already said?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Other than these two colleagues that I recognised, soldiers that belonged to a specific unit, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any officers there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard him say "ne," but I would like him to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any officers there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What did you do when you -- did you get out of the back of the truck when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a truck, the Pinzgauer. I personally went out. Some of the colleagues did not even leave the vehicle. I was standing next to the vehicle, commenting a little bit with the soldiers who were present. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you learn anything from those soldiers about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, they said that the school, as the facility, inside, is full of Muslims, that they were told to guard them there for a while, and that vehicles were supposed to come for them to be transported farther on towards Kladanj -- no, actually in the direction of Teocak. And I knew that at the time Teocak and all the time throughout the war was under the command of the Muslim forces. I don't know exactly where, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you hear any discussion between Mirko Jankovic and anyone while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I heard his conversation with one of the colleagues, actually the only one who happened to be there, Zoran Zivanovic, the talk with him, and -- and a kind of comment, and addressing the other soldiers in the group, and it referred to them in the sense, "You need to see, organise yourselves and gather up the other inhabitants to help you in this assignment." And then the part that was -- what Zoran told Mirko Jankovic boiled down that he had the desire to return with the rest of us because we already knew we were going back, those who arrived in the Pinzgauer, myself and the other comments [as interpreted] and he wanted to come back with us, and he said, "Why are they going back without me? I would like to go back with them as well. I am tired." And there that was no way that he wanted to stay. And then I stepped away and I did not follow what happened subsequently in their conversation, and I don't know what happened, whether he went back with us or Mirko in the APC. I believe that he did. Or maybe he even stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Zoran Zivanovic was a member of the Bratunac Brigade Military Police?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know, was he related to General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. We are not related. We had a member who was related to General Zivanovic, but Zoran Zivanovic that I'm talking about, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell me who the person that was related or is related to General Zivanovic, what's his name?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, Zivanovic, he was a former escort of General Zivanovic, his personal security detail, a member of his security detail at that time in the unit. As we know Zivanovic was not at that post any more from the fall of Srebrenica and onward, and then the later period after that this colleague Zivanovic, and I might remember his name before we finish, served out his term in the military police platoon together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me get you back to Rocevic, sorry about that slight distraction. When did you first hear that you were going back?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: From Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I really cannot be specific. We stayed there 10, 15, 20 minutes, not half an hour, in any event. In the beginning I tried to say I don't know why I got there, who sent us there, what the assignment was. I don't know who issued the assignment for us to return either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you do anything before you guys got in the vehicle and went back?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Other than just staying there for a bit and then commenting with the soldiers that I found there, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any bodies around?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslims, any of the Muslims around at all?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Like I said, I heard what I -- I said what I heard, but if I had a photograph of the school, the hall, and everything behind the school there are no windows so I was not in a position to see inside, but I had no doubts about believing what the people who were there said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When your group left after a short time, did the guys, the Zenica guys, stay, as far as you know? Were they there when you left?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Mirko Jankovic? Do you know where he went or what he did when you left?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I know for sure that he didn't stay behind. I don't know if we left together. I am convinced that he left a couple of minutes before we did. He switched the engine on in the APC and left in an unknown direction, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't know if he went north or south?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, really. From the place where I was, there is a small incline or a kind of mild curve from the place where I was standing on the -- next to the side of the road, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go when you left?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We took the same road that we arrived on, in the direction of Zvornik. We took the main Bijeljina-Zvornik road in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The final destination was Bratunac but we did stop by on the way, on that road. While on the way there, we didn't make any stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you stop on the way back?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We stopped in the Drinjaca neighbourhood, which is also on the Zvornik-Sarajevo road, before Konjevic Polje, near to Konjevic Polje than Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do in the Drinjaca neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We stopped in Drinjaca, before the war, and now there was a catering establishment. We stopped there. I mentioned about the way we ate in the days before that, in Potocari, food was scarce, we stopped there in order to have dinner in that catering establishment to find that because we knew once we arrived in Bratunac, this would not be waiting for us because we knew we could not achieve that anywhere else because it was late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When was the first time that you told anybody from a Tribunal about going to Rocevic, any lawyers or judges or anybody?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: This was mentioned in the B and H court in Sarajevo, and they took that seriously,. At one point I mentioned it during the proofing, for the testimony in the Blagojevic case. I told it to Mr. Michael Karnavas, when we stopped at a specific date, he took what he needed for his case, and that then there were other activities that I linked with those days immediately before the fall of Srebrenica, during and after the fall of Srebrenica. He didn't pay attention to those things. I mentioned some new information in Sarajevo that had to do with that. They listened to me. I had the opportunity to explain, and I see here, I believe that certain things will probably be left unsaid because there is a lot of that, and even during proofing with you, we didn't touch upon a lot of topics; my activities linked to those dates later and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you talk with Mirko Jankovic sometime after these events and ask him about the events?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We did talk -- well, let me say it was a kind of rebellion, a sort of negative reaction on our part, we, the policemen, at some point afterwards, a week or 10 days later, when the situation with Srebrenica calmed down a bit, when it was all over, we reacted, and I mentioned that somewhere, there was a little bit of dynamics there. Perhaps I exaggerated a little bit, but I'm right over 50 per cent, I'm certain of the facts. Our reaction about the command structure at the given point in time was we felt that we were being infringed upon at that point because at a critical point in time, we had been left without cadre, command cadres, we were left to our own devices and other units and their commanders, I don't know exactly which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you say this to Mirko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Not just myself, but other colleagues too, we told him that Slobodan Mijatovic, as the last subordinate, was not with us. There was Mirko, then Mirko's deputy, who was with them, according to their stories, and both of them were linked to Momir Nikolic. This is what they stated, that they spent those two days in the presence of Momir Nikolic which, for us, was incomprehensible for all that command cadre to be working separately, that they are all in a group together and not with the soldiers and the police. And then I added on, you probably went further from Nikolic, he's the first superior, then to Mr. Beara, and then from Beara to Mladic; this complete command cadre had distanced itself from the soldiers. They were working separately because they were telling us what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just try to clarify that. You just mentioned the name Beara. Who brought up first the name Beara in this -- in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would say, I would take that upon myself and the colleagues, that this was our revolt, our reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you mention Beara's name? Excuse me, let me just clarify that. Did you mention Beara's name or did Mirko Jankovic mention Beara's name first?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would say we. I don't mean myself personally, but I mean the colleagues and myself personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in what context was Beara brought up?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He was mentioned in the context of negative command. At that point in time, based on our conclusion, which was reflected on the situation, which reflected directly upon ourselves. You know, they are always going in a group, going from Mile Petrovic, then goes to Mirko Jankovic, they mention Mr. Nikolic, they grouped themselves, and then we add, so the command cadre as a whole functioned separately from the army. And then we add to this, where did you go and then there was the opportunity for Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Beara, I assume that the superior to him is General -- Mr. Mladic, well we couldn't link anybody else after that because there is nobody else after Mladic. Well, if -- I can explain to you what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I think I said through this, if you understood at all what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I thought you had -- you don't need any more explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, no, if you have nothing to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what if anything did Mirko Jankovic say after you and the group told him your frustrations?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He told us several times -- well, actually he was retelling us his situation, the time he spent to go from the first day, his fitness, moving, then at an APC that was captured from the UNPROFOR and that was brought somewhere. He was the only one who could actually operate it, that he was sent to various assignments in that vehicle, and in gathering some people, Muslims, groups of Muslims, escorting Nikolic, he was escorting Nikolic, as well as Mile Petrovic to Konjevic Polje several times. This is what he was talking about. These were some of his activities or their activities, their assignments. Going to the area of Zvornik with that vehicle, which I actually confirmed that for myself that there was some truth in that. He had meetings with high-ranking officers, I recall that other than Nikolic, he mentioned Pop, I don't know who he meant, Pop, Nikolic, he himself, I'm just retelling you what he said. Whereby I understand that he was justifying himself to us, that he was out on assignments, that he was talking -- that he was busy, and that was why we had been left to our own devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he say anything about Beara?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when he said pop, did you have any idea who he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I have no idea to this day. Pop in my language means priest. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At the time, did you know the commander of the -- or excuse me, did you know the chief of security of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see or -- Beara during these days, before or after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you -- did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't go into the dates, but it's definitely after the fall of Srebrenica, and in my view it was after the situation quietened down. I saw him a couple of times in front of the brigade command, and I saw him much earlier, before those events. He would come in front of the brigade command, this would be usually announced by Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now you say you saw him after things quieted down at the front of the brigade. What do you mean when you say "after things quieted down"?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I mean -- well, as far as I'm concerned, I spent the 13th, the night, I'm thinking of the 12th, the 13th, the night of the 13th, and I'm thinking of that assignment for which I said that I don't know whether this was on the 14th or the 15th, going to Rocevic. This is the last of my major assignments. As far as I'm concerned. And then after that, return from Rocevic, that's what I'm thinking of, and that's what I described as things having calmed down. I could go back. I could rest. I could relax. I mean, we did have some assignments after that but we will come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you think you saw him before or after you got back from Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of those days, I'm not thinking of that evening or the next morning, I'm thinking of those days after Rocevic, those days, that could be the 14th, the 15th, it could be the 16th, the 17th, even the 20th. I really wouldn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about Colonel Jankovic? Aside from seeing him in Potocari on the 12th and 13th, did you see him anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw Colonel Jankovic was in Potocari, just like I explained in detail how I got to him, who pointed it out to him -- him out to me, what the contact was. It was unclear to me with those papers when I was reading, with the prosecutor in the B and H court. I'm sure that I didn't understand the question. He asked me did I see him before, and I took the question to mean after because the question was put to me -- he confused me by stating his comment if Colonel Jankovic was in Potocari with a briefcase, which probably made me angry, a Colonel in that position. I would not see any colonel on the front with a briefcase. The brief case is something you would take into the parliament building or something. So he confused me a bit, so unconsciously I answered that I saw him before just in Potocari for the first time on the 12th and after that, yes, at the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear, when do you actually remember seeing Colonel Jankovic, before the two days at Potocari, 12th and 13th, or after?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I believe you mean the brigade command after those two days in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see him carrying anything?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, except in Potocari when I explained what he had of the bags, and I explained that in detail. I don't remember any details; if he was carrying a bag slung across his shoulders, a briefcase, papers, I really don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he dealing in your knowledge with any particular officer at the Bratunac command?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I know that when I saw him, he was moving. I'm going to need time if we are looking at the brigade command building, in the middle there is the kitchen, the cafeteria, the mess room, and then next the gate, the commander had his office, and then on the other side, Major Eskic had his office. I know this because we often were carrying out police jobs, and we were going in that direction, to that office, we were going to take certified requests in order to bring in military conscripts, and I saw him moving in that direction. This was when I saw him in the command sector. In the direction looking from the left of the gate, there was the office of Major Eskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Where was Momir Nikolic's office in relation to Eskic's office, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He was somewhere around in the immediate vicinity. Once I was in the room, where I encountered him, whether that was his office or not, it's something I cannot assert. It was on the opposite side from the brigade commander, closer to Eskic in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you actually see Jankovic in that sector where those offices were or just going in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I said, his movements in the direction, on the left side of the facility. So the orientation is the left side of the facility where the office was or the seat of Major Eskic. So I saw him outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he was outside the building?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you a picture. It's 65 ter 1936. It will be on Sanction again. It's page 43. Has that come up on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the person in the forefront of this picture? The big head?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the person over General Krstic's right shoulder?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember which day this was -- or excuse me, do you remember where this was?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I remember where it was. It was in Potocari, close to my workplace, let's put it that way, where the buses arrived, where the passengers boarded the buses, in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember which day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. The first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Now, I don't know if you have come to an arrangement amongst yourselves who is going to go first, second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would reduce my cross-examination but before that I would consult my -- with my client, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. You can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, let me just check, Mr. Meek, do you think you still require one hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I hope not, Your Honour. But I may need a good portion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expect it to be shorter than that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we announced that the examination would take about 45 minutes, and I believe that it will indeed be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will need 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Gvero, no cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, we won't be cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, we will not cross-examine this witness. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Will you go next, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you introduce yourself to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How are you, sir? My name is Chris Meek and I represent Ljubisa Beara. How are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've never met Ljubisa Beara, I take it, from your testimony today and your testimony in the Blagojevic trial, and your statements you gave three years after the Blagojevic trial to the Prosecutor in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you mean? I never met him? Do you mean I didn't get acquainted with him, I didn't see him around? I'm not sure what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
