utterances.text: Well, sir, you've just testified that prior to the fall of Srebrenica and sometime subsequent, you did see him around. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What was his position then?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Do you mean his position as an officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct. And with which organ?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We knew through Mr. Nikolic who performed security related duties in the Bratunac Brigade, that according to the information he provided, his superior from the staff and from the security sector was Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you have a close relationship with Mr. Nikolic of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me, you're talking about Momir Nikolic in your answer, the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: If you mean personal, close relations, well, I didn't have those with any of the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So how often would you talk to Mr. Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can state for a fact that half of his working day, Momir Nikolic spent either with the police or in front of the police building, and such like. He would go with us on regular police assignments such as taking in military conscripts and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, how often would you speak with him and converse with him on a weekly or bi-weekly basis, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You're -- you've put seeing and speaking to him in one question. I told you how many times I saw him, and I'm speaking on my -- in my own name and in the name of my unit. We were seeing him but nobody spoke to him. It was mostly he who spoke if you get my meaning. He did the talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And we are speaking of Momir Nikolic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who was your immediate supervisor or superior?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military police, in relation to these events, was after Dragisa Ivanovic, was Mirko Jankovic, after Dragisa Ivanovic. And the way we understood it in the chain of command, above Mirko Jankovic was Momir Nikolic, because we didn't have any contacts of the command of the brigade. All the assignments were given by Momir Nikolic, and he was always the one participating in them which I always found quite strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is it your understanding, sir, today, as you testify here under oath, that a security officer with the Bratunac Brigade could give orders to military police rather than make requests to the commander of the military police or the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't wish to speculate or interpret, but if you want to look at the facts, look at my statements, and who gave me orders on the 12th, 13th, and the 14th, and there you will find the answer to that. Whether this is something that was normal or not, I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you, sir. I would not like to you speculate either, but I'm afraid we are going to have to get into that since we have already. Now, you testified for Blagojevic Defence, 2004, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Said what? I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You in fact testified as a Defence witness in the Blagojevic case in this building on the 24th and 25th of May 2004, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you spent, would you agree, a substantial period of time with Blagojevic's Defence team, Mr. Karnavas, Ms. Suzana?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't agree with the statement that I spent sufficient time with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because the question was a substantial period of time, and now you're saying a sufficient time. Would you clarify that with the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My question was, sir, didn't you, from when you were first contacted by that Defence team, up and to the time that you actually gave your testimony, that you spent a substantial period of time with them, with that Defence team, irregardless of whether you felt that it was sufficient enough time. You still spent a substantial amount of time going over your proposed testimony. Would that be true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer to you in terms of substantial or not substantial. I can tell you that I had an hour's meeting with them, and then I had two contacts of one, one and a half hours each, where we actively discussed matters, and if we take into consideration that there was interpretation, there was around one or -- one to two hours discussions here and then some back in Bratunac, maybe amounting to five hours of conversation. Now, whether that's substantial or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So it's your testimony under oath here that Michael Karnavas and his co-counsel, Suzana, only spent approximately five hours total with you from the time they met you until the time they prepared you to testify in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Of active conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Then give us an idea of how many hours of inactive conversation you had with the Blagojevic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would allow me one more question on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you say inactive time or inactive hours or inactive conversation, you're not telling us that you didn't talk about the case at all or the facts that you lived through in that week or so in 1995 in July? You're not telling us that, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the time that it took us to reach the place where we had conversations, the drive to and fro of some 10 to 15 minutes because we already -- always had somebody taking us to them or from them, and then we had an exchange of pleasantries, talking about the weather, that's something that I don't factor into active conversation, talking about weather or local history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you are aware, sir, are you not, that Mr. Karnavas's client, Mr. Blagojevic, he had a defence that there was a parallel chain of command and that security was behind all of this? Do you realise that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas never talked to you about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Save for what is contained in the statement and for telling me why -- save for what is contained in the statement, he never told me what line of defence he had and how, and we never talked about those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you, sir, that you did talk about matters in relation to security officers, didn't you, during this time period of the 11th through the 17th or 18th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to Mr. Nikolic as among security officers, well, he was mentioned on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you're telling us under oath today that this Momir Nikolic is the only security officer that Michael Karnavas and his Defence team were interested in talking to you about?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I sense something quite overwhelming or overpowering from your side because in almost every question you put to me there is mention of an oath or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. You're under oath and you've testified in Sarajevo, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Now, I understand that after each question, there is mention of an oath. Yes, I did testify under oath in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, can you tell the Trial Chamber the individuals who you testified against? Could you name them, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would answer that question if the -- if Their Honours ask me about that. I have a right to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You complicated this, Mr. Meek, because he qualified it as testimony against a particular person. I would imagine that he testified about events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And about persons but not necessarily against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well that could just be a matter of the systems we come from, Your Honour, because when usually a Prosecution witness comes in a criminal case, it's to testify against an accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Meek, because yes, we don't have Prosecution and Defence witnesses here. We have witnesses on whom neither Prosecution nor defence can pretend any ownership rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir you mentioned today in your testimony a colleague, Miladin Blagojevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Not Miladin, Miladin Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse my pronunciation. And you've also mentioned another colleague of yours from 1995, Zoran Zivanovic, have you not?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In 1995, I mentioned several colleagues, not only Zoran Zivanovic. I only mentioned him in connection with one of the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, we can get through this a lot quicker if you'll just try to listen to my answer, and if you can possibly say yes or no it will be well appreciated by me and I presume everybody else here. In the case, you testified in Sarajevo, there were four accused; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One of those was Zoran Zivanovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your colleague from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Another one was Mladen Blagojevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: One of them was Mladen Blagojevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And he was also your colleague from the Bratunac Brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then we have Bozic, you can help me on this one, witness, Zdravko?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Zdravko Bozic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, he was also a colleague of yours, wasn't he, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Zeljko Zaric?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Another colleague of yours from 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And during this time period that we have been talking about today in court, you were with these folks, weren't you, these colleagues, from time to time, during those three days; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: With some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, did you have a lawyer down in there in that court at any time prior to or during your testimony against these four individuals we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Again, you're using that term "against." I don't know if that's justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm just asking you again, I don't know what term you're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was translated to me as "against."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a lawyer in the Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina any time prior to or during or after your giving testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't have contacts with any lawyers save for Mr. Prosecutor in question, before that, in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In February. And since then?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Since then, in July, I appeared in that case. I was in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you represented by a lawyer? That's my only question.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Was I represented? I wasn't the one who was tried. I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your colleagues were being tried, correct? The colleagues that you spent the time with or some of the time with in the same days you've been testifying about at the same locations you've been testifying about, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's told us already that he didn't have the assistance of counsel. So let's move to the next question, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Bear with me for a moment, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Prior to your testimony, let me ask this: Because Bratunac is not a big city, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In my mind, it is. I don't know what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Most people know everybody that's grown up there and lived there, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't make such assumptions. If you can put a specific question to me. Really I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall the time when your four colleagues that we've just mentioned were under investigation in the Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina or had just been indicted?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: My first contact with the Prosecutor in February, my only contact with anybody at that time, was when I learned that they were in detention and that an indictment had been issued against them. I was told that the Prosecutor thought my statement in that case was very important. He told me that he was representing the office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate. I wouldn't wish to offend him. I know that he's of Asian origin. He may be from China or Korea. I don't want to speculate. I have his calling card from somewhere. If I'd known I was going to need it I would have taken it with me, but I can get hold of it over the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I'll take you up on that. Did, sir, he contact you and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Since I am not living in Bratunac, for the past two years, they tried to contact me at home in January. There was a person introducing himself on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, and he came with a summons that he served -- he wanted to serve to me, but there were just my parents there. My parents kept in touch with me and at the same time I got in touch with the Bratunac SUP who told me that I was supposed to get back to them in Sarajevo. What I did, I left them my phone number and shortly after that I was -- I received a call from Sarajevo, from a person who introduced himself by the name of Brkic who said that he was working for the BH state court, and that I should appear before the BH court some time in February, I don't know the date exactly, that I should provide them with my address and I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see a copy of that summons? Was it left with the SUP or was it left at your house?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As for the summons, I was told that the summons would be served on me as soon as I arrived at the Kraljica Jelena in Sarajevo, in the building of the BH court, because I insisted on receiving the summons in order to be able to justify my absence from work. I did receive the summons in the BH court as promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And included in that summons did it tell you that you were a suspect, that they wanted to interview you as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wasn't examining the summons, but I did conclude that this was some sort of investigation, because I read on the door to the office where I was taken that it said, "Interview room" or "interrogation room," one of the two was definitely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me, sir, that you never had mentioned to Michael Karnavas or his Defence team because you say they just did not pay attention, about this alleged stories that you heard weeks later about a Pop or a Beara? You just never told them anything about that, nor did you tell anybody about it until three years later when you went down to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't have contacts about that for three years at all. After staying there in May of 2004, the first -- the next time when I talked about my participation in the events in Srebrenica was in Sarajevo in the month of February, earlier this year. To answer your previous question, that was my impression, why I was there, because during the contact I had with the person who introduced himself as the prosecutor and with the rest of his team, he told me that he needed my statement in the case Prosecutor versus Bozic et al, that I was supposed to be the future potential witness of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you understood, didn't you, that the Prosecution wanted to convict those four colleagues of yours, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It did not convict them. I don't know if they will be convicted or not. I really don't want to speculate, if they really want to convict them or not, what will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: They initiated the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How well, sir, how well, sir, did you know Jankovic before these days?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we clarify which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The commander, the new commander.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I knew him from the day that I arrived at the police in 2004. He was already in the police and that's where I met him. I'm sorry, I meant 1994. Maybe I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, and while you were in this interview in May of 2000 -- excuse me, February of -- February 5th of 2007, just this year, after having testified here in the Blagojevic case over the same facts three years earlier, towards the very end of your statement, do you recall the Prosecutor asking you, "Did you see who was in charge of these soldiers?" Meaning the -- 40 or 50 soldiers that you claim were around Rocevici.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I mentioned the figure 40 or 50, if the translation I got is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, the translation I get in English, but be that as it may, do you recall the Prosecutor, sir, asking you towards the very end of that day-long interview, question: "Did you see who was in charge of these soldiers?" Question. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your answer was, "No." Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about that. Perhaps we can move to the next question. I don't remember what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You don't remember what you said there? Are you telling me you don't remember what you said in the statement in February of this year?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are interested in any particular part of that statement, show it to him, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a B/C/S copy of it. But it's on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure it can be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The way they did this, Your Honour, they had like four sessions, and every time they will start a session they start with a new page number, 1 through whatever they get to, 25, 30, then they start at 1 again. So I think this is the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is a B/C/S, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: There is one, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could take a moment so the witness can have the copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We can give him a hard copy or would you like to put it on -- 65 ter number 2963. No. That's not it. That's Blagojevic. For the record, Your Honours, this would be page 6, starting at lower page 6 of the last section of the interview, the transcript of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it on the ELMO so that at least there is a record of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I think, witness, for you it would be lines 17. Could you read out line 17, the Prosecutor's question?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: "Did you see who was in charge of these soldiers?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What was your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The answer was, "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall, before I go any further, at the start of this conversation you had down there in Sarajevo, the BiH court, you told them you were there just to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, remember?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We are evidently misunderstanding each other. I said today too that I don't know who was in command of those soldiers. You asked me if the question was put to me, "Did I know who was in command," not what my answer was. My answer today is that I don't know. It was then the same. And much earlier than that, too. This question was also put by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, if you recalled it, why didn't you just answer it that you remember that and you said no? But I'll go on. The Prosecutor then asked you did you see any officers from any brigade? It's on the screen. And you can flip to the next page, if you want to read it. Maybe you remember your answer now. I don't know. Did that help refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We still are not understanding each other. The question put to me before that is do I recall whether the question was put to me and what the answer was. I don't remember if the question was put to me. I think this is where the -- but you are insisting that I did not answer, how I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm not insisting anything, sir. I'm just asking you -- you're looking at a transcript of your statement you gave in February of this year, that you claimed to have read and it's correct, and truthful. So we are at cross-purposes here. In any event, the Prosecutor then asked you, sir, "Did you see any officers from any brigade?" And your answer was, at the top of the next page, line 1, can you see it on the screen, sir? You can read it to yourself if you'd like to, if that refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: It would be helpful, Mr. Meek if it were read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I will, thank you,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So we can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You answered to that question, sir, whether or not you had seen any officers from the brigade. Your answer, sir, was, "Not in that moment. Definitely not. I know from the stories that later when we were coming back, that later, at the police, some officers came during the day and some of them came for sure. Jankovic mentioned it later. He commented about it, about some of his experiences and encounters with those people. I really don't know the names." You remember giving that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It's the same thing that I answered this morning. I explained all this in detail about his experiences, movements, mention of specific names like Pop and so on. But not linked directly with this person where you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That was a truthful answer that you gave back in February to the Court prosecutor in Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know which answer you mean. What I'm saying now, I stand by. I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very simple, sir. Your answer was that at that moment, you didn't see any officers from the brigade definitely not. Later you heard stories about it, and Jankovic even mentioned it to you later, when he commented on some of his experiences. Is that correct? Is that what happened? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: About the events, but I cannot link those events with the place of Rocevic, with his entire engagement over the course of the two days. Perhaps it's some other locations. I'm not connecting them with that location, those events. He never said Rocevic, Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Ljubovija, and let me not mention any more. He was talking globally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Later on, and if you'd like to, it should be on page 8 if you'd like to turn it, but let me just see if I can refresh your recollection first. It should be page 8. Okay. Now, again, the Prosecutor asked you a similar question that Mr. McCloskey asked you today, and that is, "What did Jankovic talk about when he mentioned the man nicknamed Pop?" Your answer then was, "I really don't know. He said that he was with officers, that everything -- I cannot make any guesses. First, he always praised himself. He was always with some -- we did not believe everything he said. He's the kind of person who likes to brag around. Closer he is to Momir," and that's Nikolic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: "The closer he is to Momir or someone with a rank, the better he feels. If we tried to find some logics in the whole event and answer why everything was on the police shoulder, the answer is because there was no command." Do you recall giving that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I see it, and I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And it was the truth, this guy praised himself, Jankovic, didn't he, praised himself all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That's what he used to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's what you used to say, correct? And your colleagues. You said it here, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I said that because I was present and I heard that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you also said, when you gave this truthful statement down there, that "We did not believe everything he said." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Because basically Jankovic was just one of those kind of people that wanted to go around and tell people how important they were and brag and say, I was with so and so at this date and I was with so and so at that date, to try to impress people; isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, there are a bit too many questions. According to what I said, he tended to boast to exaggerate his importance, his assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you all didn't believe everything he said?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And since you don't want to speculate, you wouldn't want to really sit here and speculate that what Jankovic told you in his braggadocio back then about Beara, was really true, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is definitely argumentative. Mr. Meek, you can rephrase your question, but he's not to answer the one as formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you this question because you are not an accused: Did you make any kind of deal with any prosecutor or prosecutors in the Court in Sarajevo not to be indicted for war crimes that occurred as your colleagues were?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, for me, this is an insulting question, and if I do not have to, I would rather not answer that question. It's absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm sorry that it insults you but frankly, a lot of times, individuals will make agreements with prosecutors so they don't become charged but yet testify in other proceedings against other people who are charged. And I believe it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that it is, and I don't see myself as a potential suspect, and from that side, I'm not afraid, and I have no deals with these gentlemen here or with Mr. Karnavas before or anything like that. Nobody ever tried to persuade me about anything or to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I know that you don't see yourself as a potential suspect, I know that Mr. Karnavas didn't, and I'm not saying that the prosecutors over here did. My question simply put: You had four colleagues from the same period of time indicted in the Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You don't get indicted. You testify in that case. And then all of a sudden, after your testimony, you bring up the name of my client and a few other people that will link, make the linkage that's possible for what this prosecutor wants in this case, and I put it to you that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already answered the question that he's made no deals with anyone, Mr. Meek. Let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again on page 7, when you're even talking with these folks in Sarajevo, you would often times say he mentioned -- again, page 7, B/C/S, line 7 for English. I'll read it out. It's after a long question by the Prosecutor, you answer a long question any way about the stories that later were coming back and Jankovic mentioned it later, the Prosecutor said: Question: "So what did he say?" Your answer was: "Well, he mentioned some officers, he said that he had contact with them, I really don't know." That was true, wasn't it? You really didn't know their names? Or were you not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You're saying I'm not speaking the truth. I'm saying now that I didn't know the names. I said then that I didn't know the names. I didn't know them then, and I don't know them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: You are confusing me after putting the question with comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I see your answer on page 64, line 4 through 6. That's fine. That's the same answer you gave back in Sarajevo, February of this year. Then, sir, you kind of indicated in that statement that the stories you heard about, and again they were stories, correct, gossip, innuendo, hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: This is his return -- well, I explained about our reaction to all of those events, the loss of command cadre. I don't want to repeat that. That was his answer, his justification, his assignments, in the course of those two days, because we literally asked him what he was doing over those two days, him and the others from the command group. Then he continued that story of his, what he was doing, and I already talked about that. I don't want to repeat that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you kind of indicated in the statement that the stories came later, we were coming back, and later at the police station, but it really wasn't that soon after the events, was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I think that you have -- well, I explained that, later, I think I explained it maybe twice from this morning, after those events when they asked me what did I think, when the situation calmed down, and thinking about the assignments of the 13th, the 14th, the 12th or the 14th and the 15th, that trip to Rocevic, and then the return, so I'm thinking of the events after those dates. I cannot say what happened before those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand that. And the events that happened before that date with Jankovic, when he wasn't around, that's the stories he's telling you about, correct? Or was it during the days, two days or so, you were at Rocevic that he wasn't there, or both? And I'll rephrase the question if you'd like me to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so because he did testify that in Rocevic he saw amongst others Jankovic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So let me get this straight. I really want to get this straight. When Jankovic is telling you subsequent to Rocevic about who he had been with, and he's naming these names, that you don't know the names, and you don't know the people, when was that time period? When did you understand that time period was, that he was talking about, when he was telling you these stories?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I answered that question ten seconds ago, that these are dates after the 15th and that the story about those dates, the stories, referred to the times when he was not with us, in answer to the put question, when he was not with us. He was not with us on the 12th, he was not with us on the 13th, and even after the 15th with the exception of that brief meeting in Rocevic on the 15th or maybe the 14th, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when did he -- when did he tell you -- strike that question. Earlier today, you testified on direct examination that you made that comment, it wasn't Jankovic, it was you who made the comment about feeling double-crossed somehow, not having a commander there and -- is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We, I said about an hour ago, us, meaning myself and my colleagues, we, not I.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you recall talking yesterday, last evening, with Mr. McCloskey, from the Prosecutor's Office, making more changes in your statements and testimony, and clarifications?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I did have a contacts yesterday, in the late afternoon, but you could say that it was more to assist with a couple of clarifications, to interpret what I meant, in those papers that arrived from Sarajevo, very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And very briefly, would you agree with the Prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey, when he says, during this brief time you spent together talking about certain issues, out of which, sir, was generated an additional proofing notes of Mile Janjic, Mr. McCloskey says, "I asked him," meaning you, "where he received the information he provided the state Prosecutor about Beara and the person named Pop. And he stated that he received that information from Mirko Jankovic one to two weeks after the events. Do you remember telling the Prosecutor that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That I said that days after those events. I'm not sure that I mentioned a week or two after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My additional proofing notes say, one to two weeks after the events.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that I specified the time. That's not clear to me. I believe that after the events or the dates after those events, or perhaps I had used the words after the situation calmed down, and I was asked what I meant by that and I responded to that question this morning. As for the rest, I really -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect, you respond to questions in different ways when you're asked by different people, but to go on, in your meeting with Mr. McCloskey yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should just be ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These kind of continuing comments will make it impossible for a witness to respond. After a while there is no point in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will not allow you to treat witnesses like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. Witness, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your time is coming up. You've got three more minutes to finish your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the Prosecutor, tells me and all the are rest of the Defence counsel representing these accused here today that you told him that you asked Mirko Jankovic where he was during the -- those days because the MPs were not happy about not having their commander with them. And then you say, Mirko Jankovic responded by bragging. Do you remember telling Mr. McCloskey that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We asked him, and not only him but the rest of the command group, including Petrovic, even that lowest ranking person, well, I cannot answer with a yes or no regardless of your nervousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can I just break in, Judge? This was a very simple question, just whether he remembered answering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have repeatedly put the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You repeatedly have the same answer, and you keep repeating, you are annoying the witness, you are annoying the Trial Chamber, and you're getting no where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, honestly I apologise for being annoying but this is the additional proofing sheet we received late last night or this morning and it's all completely new. I only have a few more questions on it. I'm just asking the witness: Do you recall telling Mr. McCloskey this yesterday? If he doesn't, he can say no. If he does, he can say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, Mr. Meek, with your last questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall yesterday telling Mr. McCloskey that Mirko Jankovic told you that he -- that during that time, he was the only person who could drive the UN APC? Do you recall that, just yes or no, talking with Mr. McCloskey about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to answer this way: He said he was the only person that managed to start up the UN vehicle. He didn't say that he was the only person that he knew how to drive it. I mean we are setting off from the assumption that we drove it frequently. Maybe then we can come to the conclusion that somebody else tried to start up the engine but he was the only one who had managed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, we are just about finished here obviously, but you did not see and you told Mr. McCloskey in the proofing session, you did not see Ljubisa Beara any time, the 11th, 12th, 13th, nor did you see him at the Hotel Fontana during the period you were there, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him at the time, in those days, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So basically what we have, and I just want to summarise this real quickly, your testimony regarding my client, Ljubisa Beara, comes from Mirko Jankovic, a person who you don't trust everything he says, he brags a lot, and he likes to be the centre of attention by throwing names out? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Except I would just add that except for seeing him after those events, the three dates. I would just add that, but I would otherwise agree with what you stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much and very quickly on that, I think you got back the 15th, correct, of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I said perhaps a hundred times about these two dates that I wasn't sure whether it was the 14th or the 15th. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you were off for a few days after being on call, on duty, all this time, weren't you? I think you testified you had a few light duties but you had some time off?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I had some health problems in those two or three days. I was receiving an infusion in the infirmary. And then we had many assignments we had to perform in relation to Srebrenica. Nobody had ever asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How long were you in the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't say I was in the hospital. It was merely an infirmary where I was treated and sent back home to undergo the treatment that I was given, and I believe that it was whilst I was undergoing that treatment that I was called off for that assignment in Rocevic, whether somebody called me or came to pick me up. And it's again those two days. Definitely after the night of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. I don't have any further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. We will have a 25-minute break. We start at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you go next, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Janjic.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My name is Jelena Nikolic and I represent the Defence of Mr. Drago Nikolic. I want to put a couple of questions to you concerning your duty activities in the Bratunac Brigade, in the military police there. You know that the military police of the Bratunac Brigade kept diaries on daily activities where the duty officer wrote the events of the day concerning the unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit P220? 65 ter number. And it's page 6 in the B/C/S and 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is the entry for the 2nd and the 3rd of July 1995, in the military police logbook or diary. Could you please take a look at it? It's in front of you. Do you see the document there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It says here, if I'm not mistaken, "Duty officer, Mile Janjic"?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise this entry and the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I am almost certain that it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you briefly wrote what it was that happened on the 2nd and the 3rd of July 1995, what the patrol and other military police units did out in the field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 16 of the same document, in the B/C/S, and 13 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before the document appears on the screen, I will tell you that this is an entry for the 12th -- the 13th of July 1995. We can see that another duty officer is named here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Reading this entry, I found under one of the bullets that the military police, among other things, provided security to the commander Ratko Mladic and had night guard shift at the Hotel Fontana and so on and so forth. Have you read this?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Is that correct? Does this reflect what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you a yes or no answer since I didn't write this document. I see just by casting one glance of it some irregularities on it, either concerning the date or -- what I want to say is that the text does not reflect what I know happened and I'm sure happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: And I mean the part of the text where it says, "Bridge, Mladen Blagojevic," although I'm sure it says Mile Janjic. It says my name on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You'll agree with me, then, won't you, that one part of the entry does reflect what happened, whereas there are some errors concerning the dates and the presence of the persons at the bridge on that date?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I connect the date, I tie it up with the presence, if I'm talking about myself personally, if it says the 12th and the 13th, that I spent those two days at the bridge and I wish I did, then I don't think the date is correct because I could not have been at the bridge on the 12th and the 13th at any time of day, not for a moment. This is unclear to me. I can only assume -- I can see that the signature is that of the duty officer, Mile Petrovic. We know also too, according to what he said, that he had great assignments with Mirko Jankovic and Momir Nikolic and others. I believe that the document may have been written subsequently, that the diary may have been supplemented subsequently. What's unclear to me is the UNHCR. I don't know anything about that. The security for the UNHCR, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But on that date, you were on duty at Fontana and you were providing security for Ratko Mladic on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th, I was securing the area there at Fontana, and in Potocari, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the same document but page 19 in the B/C/S and 16 in the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, do you see the document before you? Again, this is an entry, if the date is correct, for the 17th of July 1995. Again some of the duties of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the entire page, can we scroll the page down for him to read the entirety of the text? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I see that you were not on duty on that day. Your name is not mentioned there either. However, in one section of it, we have an entry, by a third person, that one of the activities on that date was the going to the, to Pilica, in the territory of Zvornik municipality of a group of military police. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that these other entries are also authentic although you did not write them in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, by the very fact that I wasn't there, that I wasn't mentioned, I wouldn't be able to say anything about this document authored by someone else. I cannot either confirm or deny that they were there or not. It does look and appear like a regular police report, and that's all I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Looks like one of the regular police duties of the day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The report looks like that. Now, whether the contents are true or not, I don't want to comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to a couple of questions concerning the statement you gave or your testimony before the BH court in Sarajevo against the four of your colleagues. You've testified quite a lot about it today, and I am not going back and revisiting the same issues. We have the number of the case. You saw the minutes, that's KTRZ 132/06 of the State Court for the War Crimes in Sarajevo. The case against Blagojevic, Mladen, Zoran Zivanovic, and others. Testifying in that case, since you testified in that case, you know that your colleagues in addition to the events in the Vuk Karadzic school, they were also charged for the events at the Orahovac school based on this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that I have never seen the indictment against the four colleagues. I don't know what they were charged with. It was never read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 3D133? That's an MFI document of the 9th of May 2007. It's a Defence Exhibit that was admitted through a different witness. Can the B/C/S version be shown to the witness, please? Can we turn to -- do we have the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it available or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Here it is. You see the document before you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've been reading it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We can turn to the following page, to shorten the procedure. You will recognise the names and the -- what is stated here is the background information concerning your colleagues. Are these the four individuals we were discussing previously?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please? You can see that this has to do with the events at Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page? If you look at item 6 and 7, where these individuals are charged with the events in Orahovac in the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's the same case in which you testified before the Court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is the first time I'm looking at the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you did not testify in relation to these events; rather only in relation to the events in the Vuk Karadzic school and in relation to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I have two or three questions for you concerning your trip to Rocevic. You said that six or seven of you were driving in a Pinzgauer vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the vehicle for us, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It's a military vehicle, the Pinzgauer. At the front it had a cab seating two, driver and the passenger next to the driver. At the back it did not have a tarpaulin. It was an open-type vehicle. And it had two parallel benches, laterally, with the mounted anti-aircraft machine-gun and primitively produced cover around it which could turn 360 degrees, turn on itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said today that you left off in the late afternoon hours. Can you please tell us approximately the time when it was that you set out on the 14th and the 15th of July from Bratunac and how long it took you roughly to reach that school in Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to do that but I will try. If we started off as it became dark, and it took us more than an hour and a half with that sort of vehicle to reach Rocevici. It could have been 8.00 in the afternoon, 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That we set off. That we set off from Bratunac, around -- at around 7.00. I'm saying this because I know that it was already dark as we were going back, and if we know that in the summer time it becomes dark at around 9.30, then that would be roughly it. I'm trying to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That means that you arrived in Rocevic at around 8.30, 9.00, in the evening on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could say it was 8.30, after 8.00, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was it -- was it already getting dark at the point?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't dark at the time. It was when we were going back, so in Drinjaca, as we were one hour into our trip, it was already dark. So we could perhaps say that we set out from there at around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that it roughly took an hour, an hour and a half, both ways, for the trip, Bratunac-Zvornik-Rocevic and back?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would say both -- for both ways, it took you that amount of time in one way and back, if you're taking the same route, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you taking the same route that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As we were going off on our assignment, we took one route, and then as we were going back, we partly took the same route and partly took a different route to the same destination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where was it that you changed the route and to what destination was it and why, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: On our way back from Rocevici, we reached Zvornik. That was the first large town. And then from Zvornik we were using the Zvornik-Sarajevo road, and stopped at Drinjaca, which is a small place. There, we made a stop, we had our supper there, I said this already, and it was already pitch dark at the time. And then we took a different route to go back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was it a longer or a shorter route? How long did it take you, along this route?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: From there to Bratunac, it's a longer route. It's mostly a macadam road, a dirt road, and we had to move more slowly, and it took us longer than it did when we were going from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Why did you choose that other route? Why didn't you take the regular Konjevic Polje-Bratunac route?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I said, the head of our party was Slobodan Mijatovic, who was a squad commander. That was down to him. We were told that for security reasons, we should go back along that route. He told us that but he didn't tell us who had told him that. But even if he hadn't told us that, we would have suggested that on our own. I suppose I would, and others, for security reasons. We would have decided to take that route anyway, because we knew, and we also assumed, that there would be Muslim forces crossing the area of Konjevic Polje, the area of Kravica, and we had had that sort of information in the course of the day anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Today, when you were testifying, several times in response to questions, without mentioning the first name of the person with the surname Nikolic, I assume that the whole time you were testifying about Mr. Momir Nikolic from the Bratunac Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Nikolic. Mr. Stojanovic, do you still require 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we will cut it short, I mean cut five or six questions out, because they were already covered in a way, so I think that our cross-examination will be a bit shorter than planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By how much?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my estimate, Your Honours, I think we will need 30 to 35 minutes because right now, it's very hard for me to say exactly how much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Madam Fauveau, are you in a position to go ahead with your cross-examination now? Because you said you needed 20 minutes, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In that case, I would like to discuss this with my colleague, Mr. Stojanovic, to see if that's all right to him. As far as I'm concerned it doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if you wish to have a tete-a-tete, consultation, of course, please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It seems we are going ahead with the Miletic Defence team cross-examination. Madam Fauveau, if you could introduce yourself?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic and I represent General Miletic. I would like to ask you a few questions relating to the 11th of July 1995, at the time you were going on the road to [indiscernible] Pribicevac, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to apologise. We cannot really see each other. I'm just perhaps I can ask the gentleman because I'm just answering blind like this. Well, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you were on this road, the NATO planes were flying over the area, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: If we are thinking about the 11th, at one point, they were flying over, not the whole day. I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At one point in time they were dropping bombs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether these bombs killed anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that information. I know people were killed in that action, but I don't have any specific facts, whether this was from bombs or in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But at any rate, some bombs fell not very far from your positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I tried to explain that before. Practically all the bombs, the bulk of the bombs, dropped, I believe, missing the target that was intended, the command, and where the General Mladic was present as well, this was the 3rd Battalion command. Since we were at a higher elevation, some two kilometres away from the command, the bulk of the bombs actually dropped in our immediate vicinity, having missed their target. I believe that they were the target.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you a few questions about the night of the 13th in Bratunac. During that night, you heard shots, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But you don't know whether anyone was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And just before you heard these shots, you heard screams. Can you determine whether those cries came from Muslim or Serb prisoners or was it both?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would just call that shouts, cries sounds very different. I think they were just shouts or yells, from the Muslims. Having recognised the words Glogovci, the people from Glogova, I know that Glogova is an ethnically homogeneous place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: A cry for rebellion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau needs to wait for the end of the English translation before putting her question in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, we have had some overlapping, if could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So, can we say that the shouts that you heard were a sort of a call for a rebellion?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you testified in the Blagojevic case, 24th of May 2005, this is on page 9799, you spoke of the end of the evacuation of Potocari of the Muslim population of Potocari, and you indicated that you left with Colonel Jankovic from Potocari heading towards Srebrenica to see if there were other people who wanted to be transported towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Just a correction. I received translation with Colonel Jankovic, and this is not correct, went in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sorry, my mistake. So you personally indeed left in the direction of Srebrenica from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And it was to see whether there was still people, Muslims, who wished to leave, who wished to be evacuated from the region?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I would say see and inform them about what we were given. We told them about the assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, you were to tell them that if they wanted to be evacuated,, they had to report to a specific bridge the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Statement, I'm asking if that was the information he was to give to these people. This is a cross-examination so I'm entitled to put these questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She's not allowed to misstate his evidence. He's been very clear on that point. She can ask him if there is any further information such as what she said, but she cannot put words in his mouth that he did not put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But where is the misstatement? Because I don't think that is clear in Madam Fauveau's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he has always said that it was his job to go inform people that he saw that they should go to the checkpoint in Potocari to be transported. He has never added the part that she added about if they want to go. I think she can ask him about that, but she cannot put words in his mouth that he hasn't said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not claiming that the witness said that. I'm asking him if that indeed was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are all in agreement here that forget about the question of whether they wanted or did not want to go, but please answer Madam Fauveau's question. Will you repeat it, Madam Fauveau? Because I think we have lost track.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when you went from Potocari to Srebrenica, was your assignment to say to people who wished to leave, who wanted to be evacuated, that the buses would be in a specific place the next morning and that people had to be at that spot if they wished to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The exact order, and I recall it, was that after the questions do I -- do I, and my colleague have a vehicle, then we would go in the direction of Srebrenica, not Srebrenica itself. We were told to go into the depth, in the direction of Srebrenica, and if groups were arriving, conditionally speaking, people, meaning men, women, children, that they should assemble without a panic at the gathering point in Potocari, and that the next day, transport will be organised, that buses will come, and nobody should be left behind and there should be no room for panic. And this is what we did. And this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Indeed, you didn't assemble these people. You didn't collect them and transport them yourself to this place?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, the answer imposes itself, that I went with my colleague, a police officer, and we were told to inform them, not to assemble them or transport them. You cannot say assemble them. Perhaps they weren't even there. Just the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And none of these people were forced to go to this place?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely no. I'm talking about my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show the witness Exhibit P113.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before this exhibit arrives, is it true that when you were in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July 1995, you didn't see that the Muslim population was mistreated or abused?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any abuse or mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you've seen this exhibit when you testified in the Blagojevic case. This is a - can we show the foot of the page, please - of a report of the 13th of July 1995, sent on the 14th of July at midnight, 0030 hours, from Colonel Jankovic. If you could look at the last paragraph of this exhibit. And in particular, the final two lines of this paragraph, it appears in this exhibit, at least Colonel Jankovic was convinced that the Muslim population had received adequate treatment in Potocari. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We can see here that we are talking about the 13th, in the evening. I agree with that. This is what I'm talking about. I answered that a couple of seconds ago, that I didn't see any beating, anything unusual. I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned today, this was on page 23, lines 21 and -- 20 and 21, the white house where the men were taken separately. Can you tell me, when you heard this expression for the first time, the white house?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I've never heard the term "white house." Maybe in my statements they asked me to explain about the building, where it was, what does it look like, what is the colour, whether it's yellow, blue, green, white. I tried to explain that it was a white house. But I don't know where this term "white house" comes from. I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So today, you clearly stated, and I quote from the record, page 23, lines 20 to 21, "[In English] There was the white house." [Interpretation] Indeed, so it's the first -- today is the first time that you mention the white house, that you use that term. So I'd like to know if someone spoke to you about the white house between your testimony in 2004 and today.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood my answer. I said that they asked me where these men were, so I repeat, I had to explain the building where it was near what, and the building, let's say the house, if it was a house, the colour of the house, the yard. I explained everything in detail. So it's not true that I have just heard the term "white house." I described it like that in 2004, how that house looks like, that it's white in colour, that it has a yard around it and so on, so I don't want to take up any more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, precisely. I'll read what you said in 2004. "[In English] So it's on the right-hand side, there was a big building there too. Now, was it a house or what kind of building it was, a factory, whatever, I don't know. They were brought into the yard of the particular building." [Interpretation] So back then, you didn't -- you weren't able to determine whether it was a house or a factory. Today, you used the term, the "white house," so I'm asking you once again, do you recall that someone, when you spoke with the Prosecutor here in The Hague or in BH, someone spoke to you about the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I absolutely with that -- if you go further somewhere in the statement you must have that, that the photograph of that house was shown to me, that I recognised it, that there was talk about baggage left at the gates. I was shown a photograph of that house, and I had to establish that it was that house, and that I clearly saw it in the photograph. I think the misunderstanding is there, but "white house" doesn't mean anything to me. But it was white, the majority of them were white.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Your Honour, another two or three minutes, perhaps we can end tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll adjourn here. There is no problem. You will continue tomorrow, Madam Fauveau. And then you, Mr. Stojanovic. Tomorrow, the sitting is in the afternoon, as you -- I'm sure you are aware. And we'll finish with this witness and have the next one ready, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
